svg.aria-label: Diagram: Microsoft Entra Domain Services compared with self-managed Active Directory Domain Services on Azure VMs. A managed domain creates two domain controllers for redundancy that administrators cannot sign in to, requiring a separate management virtual machine joined to the domain running the regular AD DS tools. Synchronization is one way only from Microsoft Entra ID to the managed domain, with no synchronization back, an initial sync taking a few hours to a couple of days, and the managed domain being largely read-only apart from custom organizational units. The managed domain supports domain join, NTLM and Kerberos authentication, Group Policy, custom OU structure, secure LDAP, LDAP read, and LDAP write within the managed domain only, and forest trusts on the Enterprise SKU. It does not support schema extensions, Domain or Enterprise administrator privileges, or account-based Kerberos constrained delegation, offering only resource-based delegation. Things that do not arrive from on-premises include Group Policy objects, the Sysvol folder contents, computer objects, organizational unit structures and existing SidHistory attributes, while the primary SID is regenerated in a different SID namespace and SidHistory is set from the on-premises primary SID so resources do not need re-ACLing. A cloud-only user is not synchronized until they change their password, because that is what generates the NTLM and Kerberos hashes, and a federated tenant using AD FS has no valid hash so Domain Services cannot validate credentials. SAMAccountName is autogenerated when the mailNickname or UPN prefix exceeds the 20 character limit. The three SKUs are Standard for up to 25,000 objects and 3,000 authentications per hour with backups every five days, Enterprise for 25,001 to 100,000 objects and 3,001 to 10,000 authentications per hour with backups every three days, and Premium for 100,001 to 500,000 objects and 10,001 to 70,000 authentications per hour with daily backups retained seven days and every third retained 30 days. The recovery objectives are a recovery point of five days before the event and a recovery time of two hours to four days depending on tenant size.
svg.title: A managed domain is a one-way projection of the tenant, and everything else follows from that
svg.text: Not “AD without the servers”. A read-only Kerberos and LDAP projection of your tenant.
“You can’t make changes to user attributes, user passwords, or group memberships within a managed domain.”
What you give up is, in every case, a write

In exchange: no VMs, no Windows Server OS, no DCs to patch, and “no AD forests, domain, sites, and replication links to
design and maintain.” Two DCs are created for redundancy — and “you can’t sign in to these DCs”: you build a joined
management VM and run the ordinary AD tools from there, which is a privileged host you now own.
What does not arrive from on-premises
OU hierarchy — “the managed domain flattens any
hierarchical OU structures”; all of it lands in AADDC Users
Group Policy objects · Sysvol contents · computer objects
Existing SidHistory attributes — so a prior migration’s
SID chain is lost, one generation deep only
But SidHistory IS set from the on-premises primary SID,
so “you don’t need to re-ACL resources” — the single most
useful thing here for a lift-and-shift.
SAMAccountName is autogenerated past 20 characters.
The prerequisite that is easy to miss
A cloud-only user is “not synchronized to Domain Services
until they change their password” — that change is what
generates the NTLM and Kerberos hashes.
So enabling the feature does not populate the domain with
your users. It populates it with whoever reset since.
And federated with AD FS: “there’s no (current/valid)
password hash available… Domain Services won’t be able
to validate the users credentials.”
Fourth feature in this block to depend on hash sync, after
ID Protection, outage resilience and Seamless SSO.
The SKU is three decisions wearing one name: capacity, trusts, and recovery point
SKU
OBJECTS
AUTHENTICATIONS / HOUR
BACKUP FREQUENCY
Standard
up to 25,000
up to 3,000
every five days
Enterprise
every three days
Premium
daily, kept seven days
These are “recommended capacity guidance rather than enforced limits”, so exceeding one degrades rather than errors.
The useful consequence: a better SKU buys a better recovery point. Nothing else you can do will.
Recovery is a support case, and it is measured in days
A DC restore, a corruption, or a compromised domain: RPO “five days before the occurrence of the event”, RTO
“two hours to four days, depending on tenant size” — and “Microsoft Entra support can assist you in restoring”.
Deleting the domain is a one-way door: the stored hashes go with it, cannot be reused, and every cloud user must
change their password again. Switch SKU in place instead.
The containment argument, which self-managed DCs cannot make: “any issues in a managed domain don’t impact
Microsoft Entra ID or on-premises AD DS environments.” Less capable, better contained. That is the real trade.
Sources: Compare Microsoft directory-based services, How synchronization works in a managed domain, and Management concepts for Domain Services, on Microsoft Learn.
